**What the peers said**

Both peer responses agree on the same core points:

| Point | Peer 1 | Peer 2 |
|------|--------|--------|
| Adult skull size – biparietal ≈ 14‑15 cm, smallest rigid cross‑section ≳ 12 cm | ✔ | ✔ |
| Pelvic inlet – transverse ≈ 12‑13 cm, AP ≈ 10‑11 cm | ✔ | ✔ |
| Adult skull is completely ossified, cannot mould like a newborn skull | ✔ | ✔ |
| Soft‑tissue dilation of the vagina tops out at ≈ 10 cm; bony pelvis cannot expand | ✔ | ✔ |
| Even extreme anatomical variation does not close the size gap | ✔ | ✔ |
| Only way to make it work would be to destroy either the skull or the pelvis, which violates the premise of an “intact” skull passing through an “intact” canal | ✔ | ✔ |

Both conclude **No**.

**Additional details that reinforce the conclusion**

1. **Obstetric conjugate (true AP diameter)** – the narrowest anteroposterior passage through the pelvic inlet. In a typical gynecoid pelvis it averages **11 cm** (range 9.5–12 cm). The smallest adult skull AP dimension (sub‑occipitobregmatic) is about **9.5–10 cm**, but that is measured at the very front of the skull; the overall vault height (~13 cm) then becomes the limiting dimension when the skull is turned edge‑on. Thus the skull cannot be oriented to make the 9.5 cm dimension the only one that matters.

2. **Interspinous (transverse) diameter** – the widest bony opening of the inlet, averaging **13 cm** (range 12–14 cm). Even the largest recorded adult biparietal skull width is **≈ 15 cm**, so the transverse mismatch remains.

3. **Pelvic outlet** – the narrowest part of the birth canal is the outlet (mid‑pelvis). The obstetric outlet (distance between the ischial spines) averages **11 cm**; the soft‑tissue perineum can stretch to about **10 cm**. An adult skull would have to pass this point as well, which it cannot.

4. **Molding capacity of the fetal skull** – the newborn’s cranial vault can reduce its effective diameter by up to **30 %** because the sutures and fontanelles overlap. An adult skull has fully fused sutures; the only possible deformation would be fracture, which would destroy the “intact” condition.

5. **Extreme anatomical outliers** –  
   * The most generous pelvic inlet recorded (transverse) is **≈ 15 cm**, but the AP inlet in the same individuals never exceeds **≈ 12 cm**.  
   * The smallest adult male skulls in large anthropometric databases still have a biparietal width of **≈ 13 cm**. The overlap of these extreme tails is vanishingly rare (< 0.01 % of the population) and would still require the skull to be rotated into a position that makes its vault height the limiting dimension, which is larger than any pelvic opening.

6. **Non‑biological “hypotheticals”** – If one allows surgical osteotomy of the pelvis, crushing of the skull, or an artificial conduit, passage becomes mechanically possible, but the skull would no longer be intact and the birth canal would be destroyed. Those scenarios fall outside the intended meaning of the question.

**Bottom line**

All available anatomical data—bony dimensions, soft‑tissue stretch limits, and the rigidity of an adult cranium—show a clear size mismatch that cannot be bridged by normal physiological variation or by the modest soft‑tissue expansion that occurs in labor. The only way to achieve passage would be to break either the skull or the pelvis, which violates the premise of an “intact” skull moving through an “intact” birth canal.

**Final answer:** No
